470.title: Invisibility; strength; the elephant (3.21–3.25)
470.hook: the strangest-sounding powers yet, and a quiet rule running under them: what you hold your whole attention on, you take on
470.tomorrow: Knowledge of the cosmos, the stars, the body
470.howItsDone: In the Yoga tradition, the classical commentators treat the siddhis as real attainments, while some modern teachers read them symbolically; both tend to stress that the powers matter less than the liberation the sutras aim at.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: knowledge of others' minds, and your line, and the warning. You can know the color of a mind, not its whole story. Did you ask instead of assuming? Day four hundred seventy.
screen: `OTHER MINDS — AND THE WARNING.`

segments.voice: A four-year-old watches a nature film about elephants. For the rest of the afternoon, she is an elephant. Arm swinging as a trunk, heavy slow steps across the kitchen, a trumpet at the dog. She isn't pretending, exactly. She looked at something so completely that it moved into her body. Today's sutras sound like a fantasy novel: invisibility, the strength of an elephant. But running underneath them is a rule the four-year-old already knows.
screen: `A FILM ABOUT ELEPHANTS.` → `SHE BECOMES ONE.` → `INVISIBILITY. STRENGTH.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.21: by samyama on the form of the body, its power to be seen is held back, the light between it and the eye is cut, and the yogi can't be seen. Antardhana, disappearing. Sutra 3.22 adds knowledge of the time of one's death, from samyama on karma, fast and slow. Then two sutras that show the rule underneath. Sutra 3.23: by samyama on friendliness and the others, their strengths. You met those others in book one: friendliness, compassion, gladness, equanimity, the four attitudes toward people. Rest on friendliness completely, and you gain the strength of friendliness. Sutra 3.24: by samyama on strengths, the strength of an elephant and the like. The classical commentary adds Garuda, the great bird, and the wind. Hold the elephant's strength in samyama, and you take on that strength. And 3.25: turning the inner light outward, knowledge of what is subtle, hidden or far away. So how do you read this? The classical commentators take these as real powers that come with mastery, and some in the tradition still do. Some modern teachers read them as metaphor, and today's line invites you to try that reading. Then the rule underneath shows itself. What you hold your whole attention on, you take on. Rest on friendliness, become friendly. Rest on strength, become strong. And invisibility? One reading: the person whose ego no longer needs to be noticed walks through a room unseen, and doesn't mind. Both readings sit side by side here. The sutra lists the powers plainly, and doesn't argue.
screen: `ANTARDHANA: NOT SEEN.` · `SAMYAMA ON FRIENDLINESS, ITS STRENGTH.` · `THE STRENGTH OF AN ELEPHANT.` · `YOU TAKE ON WHAT YOU HOLD.` · then, large: `READ AS METAPHOR.`

segments.voice: Today's practice tries the rule of 3.23. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Then bring friendliness to mind, not as a word but as a feeling: the way you'd greet an old friend at the door. Hold it there. When the mind wanders, come back to that warmth. Don't force it to grow. Just keep resting on it, and notice whether a little of it settles into your own face and chest. The bell holds the time.
Invisibility. Antardhana, the first of today's powers, alongside the strength of friendliness and the strength of an elephant.
screen: `INVISIBILITY — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: read as metaphor. Today, notice what you spend your attention on, a feed, a worry, a kind person, and ask what you're taking on from it. Day four hundred seventy.

471.title: Knowledge of the cosmos, the stars, the body (3.26–3.29)
471.hook: sun, moon, pole star, navel: four sutras point samyama at the sky and then at the body, as if they were one map
471.tomorrow: The heart — knowledge of the mind
471.howItsDone: Dhruva's story is commonly told to Hindu children, and some traditional texts describe the body as a small cosmos; teachers of the Yoga Sutras read 3.26–3.29 as samyama moving from the sky to the body's center.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-ONE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: invisibility, strength, the elephant, and your line, read as metaphor. What you hold your whole attention on, you take on. What did you notice you were taking on? Day four hundred seventy-one.
screen: `READ AS METAPHOR — YOU TAKE ON WHAT YOU HOLD.`

segments.voice: The Puranas tell of a boy named Dhruva. Five years old, pushed off his father's lap by a jealous stepmother, he walks into the forest to find God. He meditates so steadily, so long, that Vishnu himself appears, and gives him a place in the sky that will never move. In the story, Dhruva becomes the pole star, the one point the whole night turns around. Look north on a clear night, and the story says you're looking at a child's steadiness. Today the Yoga Sutras point samyama at the sky, and the pole star has a sutra of its own.
screen: `A BOY PUSHED OFF A LAP.` → `STEADY IN THE FOREST.` → `THE STAR THAT NEVER MOVES.`

segments.voice: Four sutras, four objects. Sutra 3.26: by samyama on the sun, knowledge of the worlds. The classical commentary unrolls a whole cosmos here, worlds stacked above and below, oceans, mountains, heavens. Some commentators place this sun inside the body too, as an inner door of light. Sutra 3.27: on the moon, knowledge of how the stars are arranged. Sutra 3.28: on the pole star, Dhruva, knowledge of their movement. Fix on the one point that doesn't move, and you can read the motion of everything else. Then the turn. Sutra 3.29: on the wheel of the navel, knowledge of how the body is arranged. The commentary lists what it finds: three humors, wind, bile and phlegm, and seven tissues, from skin and blood to bone and marrow. Sun, moon, star, navel. Notice what Patanjali has just done. He's walked samyama from the farthest thing you can see to the center of your own belly, without a break, as if they were one map. Some Indian texts describe the body as a small cosmos, with its own sun and moon. The sutras never spell that out, but they put the stars and the navel side by side. Today's line calls it the inner map. And there's a practical lesson inside the pole star. To read movement, rest on what's still. The sailor doesn't track every wave. He finds the one star that stays, and the rest makes sense.
screen: `THE SUN: THE WORLDS.` · `THE MOON: THE STARS' ARRANGEMENT.` · `THE POLE STAR: THEIR MOVEMENT.` · `THE NAVEL: THE BODY'S ARRANGEMENT.` · then, large: `THE INNER MAP.`

segments.voice: Today's practice finds a still point. Sit steady and easy. Let your attention settle at the navel, the center of the belly, rising and falling with the breath. Let that be your pole star. Thoughts will move around it like the night sky turning. You don't have to stop them. Just keep coming back to the center, and from there, notice how everything else moves. The bell holds the time.
Knowledge of the cosmos. By samyama on sun, moon and pole star, the worlds and the stars; and on the navel, the body's own map.
screen: `KNOWLEDGE OF THE COSMOS — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the inner map. Tonight, if the sky is clear, find one steady star, or just the moon, and feel your own center while you look. Day four hundred seventy-one.

472.title: The heart — knowledge of the mind (3.34)
472.hook: after the sky and the body, samyama turns to the heart, and there, the sutra says, the mind itself is known
472.tomorrow: The powers are obstacles to samadhi
472.howItsDone: Several Hindu meditation traditions place the seat of the self or of God in the heart, and practitioners often meditate on the heart lotus, sometimes picturing their chosen deity seated there.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-TWO.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: knowledge of the cosmos, and your line, the inner map. Sun, moon, pole star, navel, one map from sky to belly. Did you find a still point to read the motion by? Day four hundred seventy-two.
screen: `THE INNER MAP — SKY TO NAVEL.`

segments.voice: Ask someone to point to themselves. Me. Watch where the finger goes. Often it isn't the forehead, where the brain is. It's the middle of the chest: me, the one who loves my kids, the one who's scared about Thursday. The finger knows something before any theory does. Yesterday samyama walked from the stars to the navel. Today it climbs a little higher, past the throat and the crown, and then settles in the place the finger points.
screen: `POINT TO YOURSELF.` → `NOT THE FOREHEAD.` → `THE MIDDLE OF THE CHEST.`

segments.voice: First a quick climb through the body. Sutra 3.30: on the hollow of the throat, hunger and thirst cease. Sutra 3.31: on the tortoise channel, below it, steadiness. Sutra 3.32: on the light in the crown of the head, the vision of the perfected ones. Sutra 3.33: or from flashes of intuition, everything. And then, 3.34. Hridaye chitta-samvit. In the heart, knowledge of the mind. Hridaya is the heart. Chitta is the mind, the whole field of thinking and feeling Patanjali has been describing since book one. Samvit is understanding, awareness. Rest samyama on the heart, and you come to know the mind itself. The classical commentary fills in the picture with an old image. In this city of Brahman, the body, there's a small dwelling shaped like a lotus. That's the heart, and that's where awareness has its seat. If you were with us for the Chandogya, back on day three hundred fifty-six, you've heard that city before. It comes from the Chandogya Upanishad, the small lotus-house with a space inside it as wide as the whole sky. The Chandogya even plays on the word itself: hridi ayam, this one is in the heart, and so it's called hridaya. So the commentary reads the sutra through a much older text. Notice the order. Sky, stars, navel, throat, crown, and the last stop is the heart. Not the head. To know the mind, Patanjali doesn't send you to think harder. He sends you to rest attention where the finger points.
screen: `THROAT, CHANNEL, CROWN.` · `HRIDAYA: THE HEART.` · `THE LOTUS-HOUSE IN THE CITY.` · `TO KNOW THE MIND, REST IN THE HEART.` · then, large: `THE HEART.`

segments.voice: Today's practice rests in the heart. Sit steady and easy. Put a hand on the center of your chest if that helps, and feel it rise and fall. Let your attention settle there, not in the head. Picture, if you like, a small lotus, and a space inside it. When thoughts come, notice them from the chest, as if the heart were watching the mind. You don't need to feel anything special. Just rest there. The bell holds the time.
The heart. Hridaya, where samyama gives knowledge of the mind, the lotus-house in the city of Brahman.
screen: `THE HEART — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the heart. Today, before one decision, small or big, drop your attention from your head to your chest for one breath, and decide from there. Day four hundred seventy-two.

473.title: The powers are obstacles to samadhi (3.37)
473.word: The powers are obstacles to sama
473.hook: in the middle of the list of powers, one sutra turns the whole list over: seen from samadhi, these are obstacles
473.howItsDone: Teachers in Hindu yoga lineages quote sutra 3.37 to warn students against seeking powers, and stories of saints praise those who had such abilities and set them aside for the sake of liberation or devotion.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-THREE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the heart, the lotus-house where samyama comes to know the mind. Did you decide one thing from your chest instead of your head? Day four hundred seventy-three.
screen: `THE HEART — KNOWLEDGE OF THE MIND.`

segments.voice: A swimmer wins gold. On the podium, the medal shines against her chest, heavy and real, and the whole stadium stands. Put that medal on her in the next race. The same gold that honored her on land would drag at her neck in the water. Same medal. In one place, a prize. In another, a weight. For days now Patanjali has been listing powers: past and future, other minds, strength, the stars, the body's map. Today, right in the middle of the list, he stops and tells you what the medal weighs in the water.
screen: `GOLD ON THE PODIUM.` → `THE SAME GOLD IN THE WATER.` → `A PRIZE, OR A WEIGHT.`

segments.voice: Two sutras set it up. Sutra 3.35: experience happens because the mind's clearest part and the true self, the seer, aren't told apart. By samyama on the seer's own purpose, the seer is known. Sutra 3.36: from that come flashes of intuition, a finer hearing, touch, sight, taste and smell. Then sutra 3.37, short and sharp. Te samadhav upasarga vyutthane siddhayah. These are obstacles in samadhi. In the outward-turned mind, they're powers. Two words carry the weight. Upasarga means an obstacle, a trouble, something that comes at you. Siddhi is an accomplishment. Patanjali applies both to the very same things. The difference is where you stand. Vyutthana, the rising-out, is the mind turned toward the world. From there, knowing the future looks like an achievement. From inside samadhi, it's a distraction, one more thing to look at when the whole point was to stop looking at things and rest as the seer. That's the warning. Notice what Patanjali doesn't say. He doesn't call the powers fake. He doesn't call them evil. He keeps listing them for most of the rest of book three. He just tells you plainly what they cost if you chase them. Tradition tells of sages who could have done something astonishing and set it aside, because it would have pulled them back out. On an ordinary Tuesday the powers look smaller: praise, being right, a clever answer. Gold on the podium. A weight in the water.
screen: `THE SEER KNOWN; SUBTLE SENSES WAKE.` · `UPASARGA: AN OBSTACLE.` · `SIDDHI: AN ACCOMPLISHMENT.` · `IT DEPENDS WHERE YOU STAND.` · then, large: `THE WARNING.`

segments.voice: Today's practice notices the shiny things. Sit steady and easy, and rest on the breath. Sooner or later a pleasant thought will arrive: something you did well, a compliment, a clever idea. Notice how it tugs, how it wants to be looked at. You don't have to push it away. Just see it as a medal, nod to it, and let your attention slip back into the water of the breath. The bell holds the time.
The powers are obstacles to samadhi. In the outward mind they're accomplishments; in absorption, they're in the way.
screen: `THE POWERS ARE OBSTACLES TO SAMADHI — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: the warning. Today, when you're praised or prove someone wrong, enjoy it for one breath, then take the medal off before the next swim. Day four hundred seventy-three.

474.title: Entering another body; levitation; radiance (3.38–3.45)
474.hook: the boldest powers in the book, read the way the classical commentators read them, inside a world where mind and body are both part of nature
474.carry: read as the tradition reads it
474.howItsDone: The classical commentaries on the Yoga Sutras treat these powers as real results of mastery within the Samkhya-Yoga view of nature, and Hindu stories of saints, such as the traditional life of Shankara, tell of such powers being used briefly and set aside.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FOUR.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: the powers are obstacles to samadhi, and your line, the warning. Gold on the podium, a weight in the water. Did you take one medal off today? Day four hundred seventy-four.
screen: `THE WARNING — A MEDAL IN THE WATER.`

segments.voice: Tradition tells a story about the great teacher Shankara. He has just won a famous debate against the scholar Mandana Mishra, and Mandana's wife, the brilliant Ubhaya Bharati, takes up the challenge herself. She asks him about love between husband and wife. Shankara, a lifelong monk, has no answer. So he asks for time. He leaves his own body in a cave, guarded by his students, and enters the body of a king who has just died. He lives as that king for a while, learns what he needs, and comes back. Today's sutras name exactly that power, and others just as startling.
screen: `A DEBATE ABOUT LOVE.` → `A MONK WITH NO ANSWER.` → `HE ENTERS A KING'S BODY.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.38: by loosening what binds the mind to one body, and knowing the mind's pathways, the mind can enter another body. Para-sharira-avesha. Sutra 3.39: by mastering udana, the upward-moving breath, there's no contact with water, mud or thorns, and the body rises. Levitation. The commentary adds that this mastery also lets one choose the moment of leaving the body at death. Sutra 3.40: by mastering samana, the breath at the body's center, radiance, a glow. Sutra 3.41: samyama on the ear and space, divine hearing. Sutra 3.42: on the body and space, and on the lightness of cotton, moving through the air. How do you hear this? A few days ago, with the elephant, the line was read as metaphor. Today's line asks for something different: read it the way the tradition reads it. And the classical commentators read it as real. That isn't as strange inside their world as it sounds in ours. In the Samkhya-Yoga picture, the mind isn't a ghost in a machine. Mind and body are both made of nature, prakriti, the mind just far subtler. So a mind that has mastered its own subtle stuff might master the coarser stuff too. Only the seer stands outside nature, and the seer has no interest in levitating. Which brings back yesterday. Sutra 3.37 called the powers just before it obstacles in samadhi, and many teachers hear that warning over this whole list. Shankara, in the story, didn't stay a king. He learned what he came for, and went back to his own body, and his work.
screen: `PARA-SHARIRA-AVESHA: ANOTHER BODY.` · `UDANA MASTERED: THE BODY RISES.` · `SAMANA MASTERED: RADIANCE.` · `MIND AND BODY, BOTH OF NATURE.` · then, large: `READ AS THE TRADITION READS IT.`

segments.voice: Today's practice feels lightness, nothing more. Sit steady and easy. With each in-breath, notice the slight lift in the chest and the crown, as if the body rose a little. With each out-breath, notice it settle. Then picture a tuft of cotton, light enough to drift. Let the body feel just a little lighter, without straining for anything. If the mind reaches for something dramatic, smile at it, and come back to the plain breath. The bell holds the time.
Entering another body. The first of today's powers, with levitation and radiance, which the classical commentators read as real attainments of mastery.
screen: `ENTERING ANOTHER BODY — today's word`.

475.title: Mastery of the elements (3.44–3.46)
475.hook: samyama on the five elements brings the classic eight powers and a perfected body, and the commentary adds who doesn't use them to rearrange the world
475.howItsDone: Many Hindus honor Hanuman as the giver of the eight siddhis, and the Hanuman Chalisa is widely sung; in the Yoga tradition, the eight powers of 3.45 are understood as fruits of mastery that a practitioner is warned not to pursue for their own sake.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-FIVE.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: entering another body, and your line, read as the tradition reads it. Mind and body, both of nature. Did a strange story make more sense from the inside? Day four hundred seventy-five.
screen: `READ AS THE TRADITION READS IT.`

segments.voice: In the Ramayana, Hanuman has to cross the ocean to find Sita. He grows enormous, a mountain of a monkey, and leaps. When he lands near the golden city of Lanka, he needs the opposite. So he shrinks, small enough to slip past the guards at nightfall. Vast when the task is vast. Tiny when the task is tiny. The Hanuman Chalisa, a hymn sung in homes and temples, calls him the giver of the eight powers. Today Patanjali names where those eight come from, and adds a list for the body that sounds like a blessing.
screen: `HANUMAN GROWS VAST.` → `THEN SMALL ENOUGH TO SLIP IN.` → `THE EIGHT POWERS.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.44: by samyama on the elements in five aspects, mastery of the elements. Bhuta-jaya. The elements are the five of Indian thought: earth, water, fire, air, space. And Patanjali looks at each one five ways: its gross form, its essential nature, its subtle root, how it's woven of the three qualities, and what it's for. Earth's essential nature, says the commentary, is its solidity. Water's, its wetness. Fire's, its heat. Air's, its movement. Space's, that it's everywhere. Sutra 3.45: from this mastery comes minuteness and the rest, the perfection of the body, and freedom from being blocked by the elements. The commentary lists the eight: becoming tiny, becoming light, becoming vast, reaching anything, getting what one wills, control, lordship, and fulfilling one's resolve. The eight of the hymn. Sutra 3.46 says what the perfected body is: beauty, grace, strength, and a hardness like a diamond. Today's line: the body's perfection. Then the commentary adds a line worth remembering. Even though such a yogi could, they don't overturn the order of things, because that order was set by the will of one perfected long before. Later commentators name that one Ishvara. Total mastery, and the master leaves the world's order alone. And remember where this list sits: right after 3.37, the warning. Even a diamond body is an obstacle in samadhi.

476.title: Mastery of the senses (3.47–3.48)
476.hook: after the elements, samyama turns from what is sensed to the senses themselves, and the mind gets swift as thought
476.tomorrow: Omniscience — and the invitation of the gods, refused
476.howItsDone: Teachers of the Yoga Sutras present mastery of the senses as samyama moving from the objects of perception to perception itself, and in practice students often begin by attending to the act of hearing or seeing rather than its content.

screen: `DAY FOUR-HUNDRED-SEVENTY-SIX.`

segments.voice: Yesterday: mastery of the elements, and your line, the body's perfection. The eight powers, and a master who leaves the world's order alone. Day four hundred seventy-six, the end of a week.
screen: `THE ELEMENTS — THE BODY'S PERFECTION.`

segments.voice: A piano tuner sits at an old upright and strikes two strings that should match. To a casual ear, they sound the same. To him, there's a slow wobble between them, a wah, wah, wah, and he turns the pin until it stops. His ears may be no sharper than anyone's. He's spent years paying attention to hearing itself, not just to music. Yesterday, samyama rested on the elements, the things the senses meet. Today it turns around and rests on the senses themselves.
screen: `TWO STRINGS THAT SHOULD MATCH.` → `A SLOW WOBBLE.` → `ATTENTION TO HEARING ITSELF.`

segments.voice: Sutra 3.47: by samyama on the senses in five aspects, mastery of the senses. Indriya-jaya. The five aspects mirror yesterday's. First, the act of grasping: seeing, hearing, touching as they happen. Then the sense's own nature. Then I-ness, the sense of me that says I see. Then how it's woven of the three qualities. Then what it's for. Sutra 3.48 says what follows: a swiftness like the mind, perceiving without the bodily instruments, and mastery over primal nature itself. Notice the shape Patanjali is building. Yesterday the elements: what is known. Today the senses: the knowing. And tomorrow the one who knows. You met those three together back in book one, where the clear crystal takes the color of whatever it rests on: the knower, the knowing, the known. Book three walks right through them, from outside in. Now the week, from the top. Invisibility, strength and the elephant, read as metaphor. The sky and the body as one inner map. The heart, where the mind is known. Then the warning, at the center: the powers are obstacles to samadhi. Entering another body, read as the tradition reads it. The elements mastered. And today, the senses. A whole week of astonishing powers, and the line it turns on is the one that said: don't stop here.
screen: `INDRIYA-JAYA: MASTERY OF SENSES.` · `GRASPING, NATURE, I-NESS.` · `SWIFT AS THE MIND.` · `KNOWN, KNOWING, THEN THE KNOWER.` · `THE WEEK, FROM THE TOP.` · then, large: `THE SENSES.`

segments.voice: Today's practice listens to listening. Sit steady and easy. Let sounds come: a car, a fan, your own breath. Now shift your attention from the sounds to the hearing. Notice that hearing is already happening before you name anything. Then notice the little voice that says, I hear. Let the sounds, the hearing and the I sit side by side, without sorting them out. The bell holds the time.
Mastery of the senses. Indriya-jaya, by samyama on the senses in five aspects, bringing a mind as swift as thought.
